title: Ultrasound and needle guided spinal anesthesia
summary:
The purpose of this clinical study is to compare an ultrasound-guided spinal anesthesia procedure (Group B) and the conventional landmark technique (Group A).
Spinal anesthesia describes an anesthetic technique in which a local anesthetic is injected by puncturing the spinal cord canal (= spinal canal, space filled with nerve fluid) using a very thin needle, which numbs the spinal cord and the nerves coming from it. In this way, operations on the lower half of the body can be carried out without "general anesthesia" and without pain at the same time. The term landmark technique describes the method of finding the desired puncture site that has been tried and tested for over a hundred years. The upper edge of your pelvic bone is palpated on both sides and a connecting line is drawn between the two sides. At the intersection with the spine, a nearby space between the spinous processes (palpable bony prominences in the middle of the spine) is palpated in order to then perform the puncture at this point.
Ultrasonography of the spine and ultrasound-guided puncture can make spinal anesthesia easier to perform for several reasons. The aim of this study is to find out to what extent ultrasound and the use of a needle guide are helpful and useful and represent an improvement in the anesthesiological procedure for the patient.

A total of 120 patients in two groups (as described above) are to be included in the study.
conditions: no specific disease or health problem is examined.It is an anesthesiological procedure that is or can be used in a large number of operations.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age >= 60 years
2. Patient consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Age < 60 years old
2. Rejection by the patient
3. Allergies to local anesthetics
4. Care of the patient
5. Contraindications for spinal anesthesia
